lines.text: The camp was a stone hut, half swallowed by the ice. Its door hadn't been opened in years.
Wren went in first. She didn't wait for anyone.
Inside, everything was where its owner had left it. A cold fire pit. A cooking pot. A bow on the wall, and a quiver of arrows.
That's my father's bow.
The arrows were fletched with grey goose feathers, bound with red thread. Wren fletched hers exactly the same way. He had taught her.
He went hunting five winters ago. He said he'd be back in ten days. I was twelve.
Under the bunk, wrapped in oilskin, Ilse found a journal.
Every winter, he set a stone at the edge of the White, and paced how far it had moved since the last one.
Three hundred paces south. Then six hundred. Then a thousand. The White moves south every winter. And faster every year.
A hunter keeping records like a scholar.
He wanted to know why the game was leaving. He always wanted to know why.
The last page was different. The writing shook, and a dark stain had soaked into one corner.
Something in the deep ice. Can't see from the left eye. If anyone finds this, tell Wren...
That was all. The rest of the page was empty.
Wren didn't cry. She didn't say anything at all. She just sat on her father's bunk and held his bow.
Nobody knew what to say. So Dunn did what Dunn always does.
I'll make soup. Everybody likes soup. Even sad people. Especially sad people.
It was terrible soup. Wren ate two bowls.
That night she slept with the bow beside her. I didn't sleep much at all.
By the door, Kell sat turning one of the red-thread arrows in his fingers. Over and over.
Kell? Is something wrong?
No, Warm One. Sleep.
He set the arrow down very carefully, as if it belonged to someone. Then he looked across the fire at Wren, the way you look at someone you're about to give very good news. Or very bad.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter thirty-two, coming soon.
